body:
Chapter Eight

The Prince's Design

The first thing Outland took from Falanaras was the horizon.

He came through the Dark Portal expecting distance. Instead the world ended in torn red shelves beneath a sky split open by green fire. Fragments of land hung far above Hellfire Peninsula, their undersides trailing dust into emptiness. Beyond them, the Twisting Nether burned through wounds no cloud could cover. The sight gave his eyes nowhere safe to rest.

Then heat struck through his armor, dry enough to strip the wet from his mouth. His boots found black stone. The Portal released the rest of his file behind him in measured intervals: armor, glaives, pale faces washed green by the threshold. One spellbreaker stumbled and recovered before Daric could catch him. No one laughed.

“Count,” Falanaras ordered.

Names passed down the line. Twelve answered. Captain Althene’s rangers emerged next, already turning toward the broken ridges with bows half raised. Rommath and the magisters stood beside a bank of Outland machinery whose crystal housings throbbed in answer to the Portal. Astalor had one case open and both hands buried among the instruments. Selorien held the other case beneath his arm while recording figures on his slate.

The reception awaiting them consisted of twenty blood elf soldiers, two wagons, and a captain with a bandage darkening beneath his left pauldron. Their armor carried the prince’s phoenix, scored by travel and battle. No musicians sounded a welcome. No standard dipped for the company that had crossed a world in answer to Kael’thas’s summons.

The wounded captain saluted Rommath. “Grand Magister. The route west remains passable. We lost two outriders yesterday and drove off a fel orc patrol before dawn. If we leave within the hour, we can make the ravine camp before dark.”

Rommath looked beyond him. “Where is His Highness?”

“Netherstorm. The campaign moved before your departure message reached us.” The captain’s gaze touched Liadrin, Astalor, and the sealed wagons. “The prince ordered us to bring you through without delay.”

Falanaras had carried the summons down an entire continent and through the Dark Portal. Some quiet part of him had still expected Kael’thas to stand on the far side, bright-haired and impossible, ready to explain why Rynel had been worth calling from the Ghostlands. The foolishness of that expectation became obvious only after it failed.

Althene stopped beside him. Her eyes had not left the ridges. “You look disappointed.”

“I look overheated.”

“Already? Outland will take that personally.” She turned to her rangers. “Water now. Cloaks over the bowstrings. If the air smells sweet, call a magister before breathing deeply.”

They formed under a sun that seemed too small for the heat it gave. As the Portal shrank behind them, Falanaras looked back once. The green threshold stood inside its stone arch, the only whole thing in sight. Azeroth waited beyond it, close enough to cross and already unreachable by any ordinary road.

The column marched west.

***

Hellfire Peninsula taught them its distances by withholding shade.

For three days the escort led them between scorched ridges, shattered siegeworks, and pits where old bombardments had fused sand into dark glass. Fel iron spikes rose from abandoned fortifications. Once they passed a field of bones too broad to belong to a single battle. The Outland soldiers did not slow or name the armies that had died there.

The magical hunger changed in that wounded country. Power saturated the air in violent traces—fel seepage, old wards, ruptured currents from the Nether—yet little of it could be taken safely. Every breath carried the scent of a feast laid behind locked iron. Rommath ordered smaller, more frequent rations. Soldiers accepted crystals without comment and watched one another’s hands afterward.

At the ravine camp, Falanaras found the prince’s soldiers sleeping in armor beside ward pylons patched with draenei metal and demon hide. Their quartermaster greeted the newcomers by name, found Daric a whetstone, and pressed a cup of bitter stimulant into Althene’s hand before she asked. It felt almost like a Silvermoon post until a pair of broken draenei constructs passed overhead under blood elf control, their blue cores caged inside crimson bindings.

“Salvage?” Falanaras asked the escort captain.

“A useful word.” The captain tightened the bandage beneath his pauldron. “Out here, ownership lasts until someone stronger arrives.”

On the fourth day, red stone gave way to a descent where the air cooled and thickened. Blue growth spread across the valley below. Giant mushrooms rose through violet mist, their caps broad enough to shelter companies. Water gleamed between reeds and luminous pools. After Hellfire, the marsh looked merciful from above.

Its smell reached them first: wet earth, mineral rot, and a sweetness that coated the tongue.

Althene covered her mouth with a scarf. “Magister.”

Selorien tested the air with a silver wand. “Spores. Irritating, mildly intoxicating, and likely to produce poor judgment in anyone who mistakes pleasant for harmless.”

“That excludes the infantry,” Althene said.

Daric adjusted his scarf. “We have survived the rangers’ judgment so far.”

At the marsh road, their blood elf escort halted. Figures waited in the shallows ahead: scaled torsos rising above coils thick as ship cables, polearms held upright in four-fingered hands. Jeweled armor caught the mushroom light. Some bore the severe faces of women; others had long jaws, fins, and teeth that showed even with their mouths closed.

The naga commander inclined her head to Rommath. “The path is prepared. Lady Vashj honors the prince’s passage.” Her gaze traveled over the retinue with the slow interest of someone inspecting cargo that might prove edible. “Your landborn soldiers will remain upon the stones. The deeper pools are not forgiving.”

Falanaras looked toward Liadrin. “Do we trust them?”

“Count them,” she said. “Count the paths they offer and the ones they keep for themselves. Trust is a luxury observation may later justify.”

“The prince trusts Lady Vashj.”

“The prince accepts her aid. Those are separate acts.” Liadrin watched the naga slide aside to receive them. “Nothing in Outland is given. Someone paid.”

They entered Zangarmarsh between naga outriders who moved through water without sound. The stone path twisted among pools bright with inner color. Huge moths drifted beneath the mushroom caps, leaving silver dust behind their wings. Once, a reed bank opened to reveal huts woven around a dead fungal trunk. Broken baskets floated in the shallows. The naga passed without looking.

“Who lived there?” Falanaras asked.

The naga commander did not turn. “Those who failed to keep it.”

That night, camp stood upon an island of stone while the naga kept watch from the water. Falanaras took second patrol with Liadrin. Blue light rose around her boots. Somewhere beyond the reeds, something large disturbed the pool and settled again.

“They stripped that village,” he said.

“Probably.”

“And we march under their guard.”

Liadrin stopped at the island’s edge. “Every ruin was someone’s Quel’Thalas. Remember that before necessity makes the people beneath it too small to see.” Her reflection broke in the moving water. “Then remember that seeing them will not always give you the power to save them.”

“You make certainty sound cruel.”

“It often is. Being correct about necessity will not make terrible things less terrible.” She resumed the patrol. “Anyone who promises otherwise is selling comfort.”

***

Blade’s Edge rose from the marsh in knives.

The naga left them at the first ascent, turning back toward the water after a final exchange of sealed messages. Blood elf outriders met the column beneath a rib of stone and led them onto ledges where two soldiers could scarcely walk abreast. Spines from creatures larger than ships pierced entire mountainsides. Wind screamed through their hollow bones.

They climbed for two days. The path offered no level ground, only shelves, rope bridges, and steep cuts slick with pale dust. Falanaras moved his spellbreakers toward the column’s outer edge where their shields could catch attacks from above. Althene sent scouts ahead and lost sight of them within fifty paces whenever the trail bent.

The attack came at noon beneath a natural arch. Shadows crossed the stone. Althene shouted before Falanaras found their source.

Winged shapes folded out of the glare—black hides, hooked limbs, mouths bright with gathered flame. The first bolt struck a shield and burst green across the ledge. A soldier went down with his cloak burning. Daric dragged him against the cliff while the infantry locked shields over both of them.

“Air ward!” Falanaras drove his glaive’s lower blade into a seam in the rock. Six spellbreakers answered. Overlapping red planes rose above the file as another volley descended. The fel bolts struck armor, runed shields, and barriers trained to deny hostile magic an easy hold. Fire spread across them, hungry and corrosive, but the curse within it could not fasten to the spellbreakers beneath. Falanaras caught the leading current and opened its loose power to the whole line. Spellbreakers, infantry, and the rangers nearest the gaps drew measured threads together, thinning the volley while he turned the undrained force along the ward’s edge. Daric dragged the first burned soldier beneath the cover. Green flame still clung to the man’s cloak and tried to enter the wound. A spellbreaker hooked that completed burning into the ring of his glaive, lifted it whole from the soldier, and cast it onto a diving attacker. The creature’s own fire closed over its wings.

Rangers fired through the gaps, steadied by the stolen heat. One creature spun into the gorge with three arrows buried in its throat. The spellbreakers cast their glaives at those gathering another volley. Each blade cut hide and tore power out through the wound; fel light burst inside the attackers as their lost magic became injury. Two dropped before they could release. Another struck the barrier feetfirst, claws shrieking across the red plane. The infantry beneath it seized at the magic in its limbs, their smaller draws weakening the force that held it aloft. Falanaras released the ward, stepped beneath the falling body, and cut upward with both blades. Black blood struck the cliff. The creature crashed across the path and nearly carried him over the edge.

Daric caught the back of his harness. “Your captaincy remains experimental, sir.”

“Then preserve the evidence.”

A deeper cry rolled above them. The remaining creatures scattered as something larger passed behind the arch. Astalor raised one hand and spoke a quiet phrase. Violet force gathered around a winged attacker and tightened. Bones snapped inside the field. He let the ruined body fall, then turned the same measured attention toward the larger shadow.

The great creature plunged through the opening, all horn, membrane, and furnace light. Rommath met it with a lance of crimson fire. Liadrin stood inside the blast, braced behind her shield as the creature struck the ledge. Stone broke under its forelimbs. Falanaras saw the path collapse in pieces behind her boots.

He crossed the distance before the thought completed. A mantle of furnace fire wrapped the creature’s chest, fed its wings, and hardened the scales around its heart. Falanaras caught that active enchantment between the glaive’s blades. He took a measured surge from its outer heat to steady his grip, then stripped the mantle from the demon and cast the stolen fire across Liadrin’s shield. Her iron face burned white-green without consuming. The creature’s chest went dark and vulnerable. Liadrin drove the strengthened shield beneath its jaw. Daric’s soldiers thrust together into the exposed throat, and Althene’s arrow vanished through one cooling eye.

The creature convulsed. Falanaras tore his glaive free and brought both blades down. Its inner fire collapsed with a pressure that drove everyone to one knee.

Silence returned in fragments: first the wind, then the hiss of scorched leather, then wounded soldiers naming themselves for the count.

Falanaras helped bind the burned man Daric had pulled clear. His own hands shook when the knot was finished. The combat draw had been useful and controlled. The danger came afterward: the smell of ruptured magic filled his head, and every bright remnant in the dead creature called for him to continue though the fight was over.

Selorien crouched beside him and held out a narrow crystal. “Take it before you begin explaining why you do not require it.”

Falanaras looked toward his soldiers. Those who had drawn from the volley were already checking one another for steadiness under Althene’s supervision. Daric drank water with his back to the creature’s leaking fire, the deliberate posture of a man who had taken enough.

He closed his hand around the crystal. Arcane warmth passed into him, controlled and thin. The corpse’s pull receded, leaving the sharper recognition that his first draw had ended with the battle and his wanting had not.

Selorien watched his pupils settle. “Master Bloodsworn says a soldier who accepts the care he requires has no cause for shame.”

“And you?”

“I believe he is correct, though I resent having so little to improve upon.” Selorien rose and offered him a hand. “We still need you upright.”

They left the carcasses for the mountain and continued north.

***

Netherstorm announced itself with thunder beneath the ground.

The mountains opened onto a country broken into violet islands over an abyss. Arcane storms walked the distances in white columns. Bridges of iron and bound energy linked shelves that should have drifted apart. Far beyond them, Tempest Keep floated against the wounded sky, pale and immense, its towers lit from within by a radiance colder than sunlight.

Below the first ridge, Kael’thas had built a war.

Camps spread across three terraces behind layered wards. Smithies rang beside field hospitals. Magisters charted the storms from towers of red crystal and scavenged metal. Infantry drilled between siege engines whose frames combined Thalassian craft with parts taken from draenei constructs and demonic machines. Supply clerks moved through it all carrying tablets, ration lists, and the familiar expression of people who knew every victory depended upon someone signing for lamp oil.

The welcome there was louder than Hellfire’s. Soldiers called Rommath’s name. Officers embraced companions they had not seen since Dalaran. A magister from Silvermoon’s old western academies recognized Astalor; Astalor answered the man’s hurried greeting with a slight smile before both of them bent over a slate and began debating conduit tolerances. Someone thrust spiced wine into Daric’s hand and apologized that it came from a fungus.

Falanaras should have felt at home. Phoenix banners moved above red tents. The soldiers cursed in Thalassian when a wagon jammed. Every ward carried methods he understood, adjusted by field use until the old elegance had become spare and brutal.

Yet satyrs unloaded ammunition beside blood elf quartermasters. A felguard stood chained at a forge while smiths drew heat from the furnace burning inside its chest. Nobody stared. Nobody lowered a voice. The compromises that had followed the retinue across Outland lived here as routine.

Althene watched a young courier squeeze between the satyrs without breaking stride. “They became accustomed.”

“So did Silvermoon,” Falanaras said.

Her expression tightened. “Yes.”

That answer unsettled him more than disgust would have.

They were assigned quarters on the second terrace. Before Falanaras could remove his armor, a runner brought orders for the captains to report at dusk. He left Daric arranging the file and followed Althene toward the command ward.

A lone figure waited outside the ward-line where the stormlight struck hardest.

He was sin’dorei. The long ears, high cheekbones, and red sash left no doubt. The rest had been remade. Black cloth covered his eyes, bound beneath swept horns that rose from his brow. Fel scars crossed his bare arms and glowed in the failing light. Two crescent blades rested across his back. He faced the Netherstorm with the stillness of a sentry listening to an enemy no one else could hear.

Althene’s hand settled near her knife. “Netharel Suncleft.”

The demon hunter turned his covered gaze toward them. “Captain Starwind. You brought the homeborn through alive.” His voice remained recognizably Thalassian, though a second roughness moved beneath it.

“We had competent guides,” Althene said.

“Then Outland is becoming generous.” Netharel inclined his head toward Falanaras. “Dawnspear. You carry a dead man’s command.”

Falanaras felt the summons against his chest. “You know why we came?”

“I know why everyone comes. Need, followed by a name grand enough to command it.” The demon hunter’s mouth curved without humor. “You are wondering whether I regret what I became.”

“I did not ask.”

“You were polite enough to keep it behind your teeth.” Fel light brightened along Netharel’s scars as thunder rolled below. “Regret is for choices that can be undone. I ask whether the weapon still serves.”

“And does it?”

Netharel turned back toward the storm. “Tonight.”

The ward admitted Falanaras and Althene. Behind them, the demon hunter remained outside, guarding blood elves from dangers he had taken inside himself.

They crossed the inner court as a shivarra descended the command steps.

She towered over every elf present, blue-violet skin draped in black silk and gold chains. Six jeweled arms moved with separate grace. Two carried curved blades; another turned a goblet by its stem; the others rested empty, which made them no less threatening. Horns framed a face of severe beauty. Magisters stepped aside and bowed as she passed.

“New captains,” she said. Her attention settled on Falanaras with predatory courtesy. “Silvermoon still sends beautiful things into ugly wars. I am Xirathra.”

He gave the minimum bow owed an allied commander. “Falanaras Dawnspear.”

One of her empty hands lifted his chin before he could step away. A claw traced the air beside the scar at his jaw without touching it. “This one has begun to improve.”

Falanaras held still until she withdrew. Althene’s silence had become lethal beside him.

Xirathra smiled at them both. “The prince’s people retain their pride. Good. Pride gives pain somewhere interesting to enter.” She continued down the steps. The magisters behind her rose from their bows and resumed discussing siege intervals.

No alarm sounded. No ward rejected her. A line Silvermoon would once have guarded with fire had been crossed so often that no one heard the passage anymore.

***

The war room had been built around a captured draenei lens.

Its blue surface filled the floor and held a moving image of Tempest Keep. Towers revolved in pale light. Lines of force linked the fortress to its satellites and sank into the storms below. Red markers showed blood elf companies, siege engines, and planned breaches. Black markers named losses already accepted.

Kael’thas stood at the far edge of the lens.

Falanaras knew the prince from coins, proclamations, and portraits preserved through the fall. None had captured the force of his presence. Bright hair fell over a sweeping crimson mantle. A high red-gold guard rose above one shoulder. Three Verdant Spheres circled him in slow fire, answering his smallest movements. He wore no crown. The room had arranged itself around him without one.

Rommath stood at his right. Astalor and Selorien had already opened their cases beside Master Engineer Telonicus. High Astromancer Solarian waited over the eastern projection, her hands bright with starfire. Voren’thal the Seer watched the lens with distant, exhausted eyes. Lord Sanguinar and Thaladred the Darkener held the military side of the table. Liadrin stood among them in dark plate, the only person present whose office Falanaras could not yet name.

Kael’thas looked up as the captains entered. “You have crossed far to reach us.” His voice was quieter than Falanaras expected, carrying without effort. “Quel’Thalas has paid for every soldier in this room. I will not pretend the distance makes that debt smaller.”

His gaze found the new insignia at Falanaras’s throat. “Captain Starweaver?”

Falanaras removed the sealed summons and placed it in both hands. “Dead in service, Your Highness. He named me to answer in his place.”

Kael’thas received the case. Grief moved across his face too briefly for ceremony. “Then his last command stands. You are welcome here, Captain Dawnspear.”

Three sentences, and Rynel’s death had entered the prince’s war. Falanaras bowed. He hated how much the acknowledgment mattered.

Kael’thas turned to the lens. “We begin at dawn.”

The plan unfolded in layers. Solarian described the storm cycles that would cover the first advance. Telonicus marked the siege engines assigned to break the outer conduits. Sanguinar’s heavy infantry would draw the fortress defenders toward the southern approach while Althene’s rangers screened the western bridges. Thaladred would lead the assault through the first breach. Falanaras’s spellbreakers were assigned to the central force under Liadrin, charged with suppressing hostile wards long enough for Astalor’s magisters to enter.

Falanaras followed the sequence with a soldier’s relief. Numbers of companies, crossing times, reserves, retreat signals: these belonged to a world where danger could be divided into duties. The prince questioned every delay. Rommath challenged the mana allowances. Astalor studied one proposed conduit, then declined it. “Its failure would seal the breach team inside. The western feed will carry less power, but it leaves us a second path out.” Selorien revised the casualty estimate after hearing him.

They were prepared. More than prepared. The campaign had been waiting for the people named in the summons.

When every outer movement had been assigned, Kael’thas touched two fingers to the lens. Tempest Keep opened in luminous sections. Towers fell away. Corridors narrowed toward a central chamber buried behind the fortress defenses.

A white symbol burned there.

“The fortress matters,” the prince said, “but it is not our purpose.”

No one in the inner circle reacted. Liadrin’s hands remained folded behind her back. Astalor watched the white mark with a scholar’s quiet wonder. The pale radiance reflected in his eyes, and his mild expression held open admiration. Falanaras understood then that some people in the room had crossed Outland already knowing what waited at the end.

Kael’thas looked around the lens. “Within the innermost sanctum is a naaru called M’uru. The naaru are living beings of the Holy Light—ancient, intelligent, and composed of the same power priests and paladins invoke. They created Tempest Keep as a fortress against the Burning Legion.”

A stir passed through the officers who had received no fuller briefing. The unfamiliar word acquired weight by degrees: living Light, housed within the pale fortress, powerful enough that Kael’thas had built an entire campaign around reaching it. Falanaras glanced at Liadrin. Her face had gone still.

Rommath spoke into the silence. “The Sunwell fed an entire civilization without conscious effort from any citizen who depended upon it. We have replaced that inheritance with crystals, scavenged currents, and methods that fail most severely among those least able to secure them. M’uru contains a stable power unlike the stores we ration now.”

Astalor adjusted the projection. Bands of crimson light appeared around the white symbol. When he spoke, his voice was soft enough that the room had to quiet for him. “M’uru is magnificent. Its power is stable at a scale no reservoir within our reach can match. The chamber readings show that a layered matrix can contain the entity and govern the current without material loss during transport. Once it is in Silvermoon, we can begin the work of distributing that power on our own terms.”

The room changed around the promise. Falanaras saw soldiers in Silvermoon straighten after feeding. He saw common quarters where children slept beside weak crystals because their parents could afford nothing stronger. He saw the fixed concentration in Rynel’s eyes inside Deatholme and the captain refusing the anchor at the end. A source that did not diminish. Power enough to quiet the hunger before it stripped another person down to appetite.

The scale of the possibility quickened his pulse. If M’uru could give what the magisters promised, children might grow without learning to hide shaking hands. Soldiers could take the field without measuring every exertion against the next ration. Rynel’s collapse would cease to be a future waiting inside anyone who misjudged one bad day. For the first time since the Sunwell’s destruction, long-term relief stood before him as more than a prince’s distant assurance.

Spellbreaker training followed close behind hope. Power on that scale would not travel quietly. A failed restraint could tear through soldiers, engines, and whatever road carried it home.

“You mean to bring it back to Silvermoon,” he said.

Sanguinar looked toward him as though a junior captain had interrupted a funeral rite. Kael’thas only nodded. “Alive and whole.”

Falanaras kept his gaze on the bands surrounding the white mark. “Can the binding survive the journey?”

Astalor indicated the bands around the white mark. “It can. The Portal crossing presents the greatest uncertainty, so the transport frame will carry an independent inner restraint and replaceable outer anchors. We need not ask one binding to survive every strain.”

“And if it resists after the breach?” Falanaras asked. Apprehension sharpened the promise rather than diminishing it. An answer powerful enough to sustain Quel’Thalas was powerful enough to destroy its escort.

The Verdant Spheres turned behind Kael’thas, casting green fire across the lens. “Then every layer of the restraint answers together. M’uru’s nature does not exempt it from force, Captain. We have mapped the chamber, measured its emissions, and built redundancy into the extraction.”

Rommath’s voice followed, hard and level. “The greater danger lies in leaving our people dependent upon failing stores because certainty was unavailable.”

“How soon after it reaches Silvermoon can the power be distributed?” Falanaras asked.

“Not immediately,” Astalor said, his manner as mild as before. “First we must establish a controlled draw and observe how quickly M’uru’s power restores itself. If direct distribution proves unstable, we will test storage vessels and wardstone relays before widening access. Our purpose is lasting mastery of the current. Relief that exhausts its source is merely another ration.”

Kael’thas enlarged the inner sanctum. “Lady Liadrin will accompany the breach team. She once served the power we intend to secure. If M’uru responds to any memory of that bond, she is best placed to read it.”

Every gaze found her.

Liadrin’s knuckles had whitened where one hand enclosed the other. She released them deliberately. The prince was sending a former high priestess into the presence of living Light, and she received the assignment as she had every other: by mastering the first visible reaction before anyone could mistake it for hesitation.

“I will go,” she said.

Her answer set the room moving again. Astalor resumed in his quiet voice, describing how the restraint pylons would overlap and how each failed layer could be replaced without opening the whole binding. Rommath revised the escort strength. Kael’thas assigned Falanaras’s file to hold the inner approach while Liadrin and the magisters entered the sanctum.

Falanaras listened and understood his place. He would hold the inner approach while the magisters secured M’uru. If they succeeded, the hunger that had governed every ration, every tremor, and every private failure since the Sunwell’s destruction might finally face something larger than endurance.

When the council ended, dawn remained several hours away. Officers carried their orders into the camp. Tempest Keep shone beyond the wards, remote and pale above the storm.

Liadrin stopped beside Falanaras at the command steps. “You asked the useful questions.”

“I would prefer our answer reach Silvermoon without killing its escort.”

“A promising instinct in a captain.” Her gaze remained on the fortress. “Do you believe it can end the hunger?”

“I believe it may be the first answer large enough.” For once, hope did not feel like a slogan sent from somewhere beyond his reach. It hung before them in the storm, guarded by walls that could be breached and measured in duties he knew how to perform.

Below them, soldiers prepared the siege. Mana crystals passed from hand to hand. Blades came free of sheaths for inspection. Magisters woke the engines one conduit at a time.

Across the broken dark, M’uru waited within the pale heart of Tempest Keep.

At dawn, they would begin the work of bringing it home.
synopsis: After arriving in Hellfire Peninsula to only a small military reception, Falanaras and the summoned retinue realize that reaching Kael'thas will require a hard journey across Outland rather than immediate revelation. Escorted first by Kael'thas's blood elves and then by naga allies through Zangarmarsh, they pass through Blade's Edge and finally reach the campaign's heavily organized staging grounds in Netherstorm, where the prince's followers feel at once familiar, welcoming, and deeply altered by the habits of survival in Outland. Encounters with Netharel Suncleft, Xirathra, and the campaign's other compromised allies sharpen Falanaras's sense of what his people may become under sufficient necessity. At last, in the war rooms before Tempest Keep, he sees Kael'thas's inner circle gathered together, hears the prince speak for the first time, and learns through detailed assault planning that the true objective hidden inside the fortress is the capture of the naaru M'uru as a lasting answer to Silvermoon's hunger.
title: Chapter 8: The Prince's Design
